subject: ELA
title: English 11 – American Literature
description: A chronological survey of American literature from Puritan writing through contemporary voices, read alongside the founding documents and speeches that shaped the nation. Students write rhetorical analyses, literary arguments, a personal narrative suitable for college applications, and a sustained research paper, with grammar and vocabulary woven into each week. Seminars and recitations build formal speaking skills.
framework: California Common Core State Standards for ELA/Literacy (grades 11–12); 2014 California ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.11-12.1: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence, including where the text leaves matters uncertain.
standards.RL.11-12.2: Determine two or more themes and analyze their development and interaction; provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.11-12.3: Analyze the impact of an author's choices about how to develop and relate elements of a story or drama.
standards.RL.11-12.4: Determine meanings of words and phrases, including figurative and connotative language, and their impact on meaning and tone.
standards.RL.11-12.5: Analyze how an author's choices concerning structure contribute to meaning and aesthetic impact.
standards.RL.11-12.6: Analyze a case in which grasping point of view requires distinguishing what is directly stated from what is meant (satire, sarcasm, irony, understatement).
standards.RL.11-12.7: Analyze multiple interpretations of a story, drama, or poem (recorded or live production), evaluating how each interprets the source text.
standards.RL.11-12.9: Demonstrate knowledge of 18th-, 19th- and early-20th-century foundational works of American literature, including how two or more texts treat similar themes.
standards.RL.11-12.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, independently and proficiently in the grades 11–CCR text complexity band.
standards.RI.11-12.1: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of informational text.
standards.RI.11-12.2: Determine two or more central ideas and analyze their development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.11-12.3: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop.
standards.RI.11-12.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including how an author refines the meaning of a key term over a text.
standards.RI.11-12.5: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument.
standards.RI.11-12.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective.
standards.RI.11-12.7: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats to address a question.
standards.RI.11-12.8: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning.
standards.RI.11-12.9: Analyze 17th-, 18th-, and 19th-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes, and rhetorical features.
standards.W.11-12.1: Write arguments to support claims using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
standards.W.11-12.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas clearly and accurately.
standards.W.11-12.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, details, and sequence.
standards.W.11-12.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
standards.W.11-12.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
standards.W.11-12.6: Use technology to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products.
standards.W.11-12.7: Conduct short and sustained research projects to answer a question or solve a problem, synthesizing multiple sources.
standards.W.11-12.8: Gather relevant information from authoritative print and digital sources, assess strengths and limitations, and integrate information avoiding plagiarism.
standards.W.11-12.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
standards.W.11-12.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
standards.SL.11-12.1: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
standards.SL.11-12.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.
standards.SL.11-12.4: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence conveying a clear and distinct perspective.
standards.SL.11-12.5: Make strategic use of digital media in presentations to enhance understanding and add interest.
standards.SL.11-12.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English.
standards.L.11-12.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage; observe hyphenation conventions and resolve usage issues with references.
standards.L.11-12.2: Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation, and spelling conventions.
standards.L.11-12.3: Apply knowledge of language to understand how it functions in different contexts and to vary syntax for effect.
standards.L.11-12.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words using context, word parts, and reference materials.
standards.L.11-12.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
standards.L.11-12.6: Acquire and use accurately general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: Puritan and Colonial Voices
units.big_idea: Early American writing reveals how faith, fear, and community shaped a new society—and how drama can use that past to critique the present.

units.title: The Rhetoric of Revolution
units.big_idea: The founders used persuasion and reasoned argument to justify independence and define American ideals.

units.title: Romanticism and Transcendentalism
units.big_idea: American Romantics celebrated the individual, nature, and intuition while Dark Romantics probed sin and the irrational.

units.title: Voices of Freedom: Slavery and Civil War
units.big_idea: Enslaved and free Americans used narrative and oratory to claim the nation's promise of liberty.

units.title: Realism and Regionalism
units.big_idea: After the Civil War, writers turned to ordinary lives, local speech, and the gap between ideals and reality.

units.title: Modernism and the Harlem Renaissance
units.big_idea: Modern writers fractured old forms to capture disillusionment, the city, and the search for identity and the American Dream.

units.title: The Research Paper
units.big_idea: Sustained research means asking a real question, weighing sources, and building an original argument with honest citation.

units.title: Mid-Century America: Drama and Civil Rights
units.big_idea: Postwar drama and civil rights rhetoric tested whether the American Dream was open to all.

units.title: Contemporary and Diverse American Voices
units.big_idea: Contemporary writers expand who tells the American story, exploring language, memory, war, and belonging.

units.title: Synthesis and Final Portfolio
units.big_idea: Revisiting the year's texts shows how American literature argues with itself across centuries.

weeks.topic: Origins: Native American and Puritan narratives
objectives: Compare an Iroquois creation story with Bradford's account
materials: The Iroquois Constitution excerpt / 'The World on the Turtle's Back'

days.title: Course launch
days.work: Set up a reading journal and take a 20-minute diagnostic writing sample responding to 'What makes someone an American?'

days.title: Creation story
days.work: Read 'The World on the Turtle's Back' and annotate values it reveals; write a 150-word objective summary.

days.title: Of Plymouth Plantation
days.work: Read Bradford's chapters on the Mayflower voyage and first winter; chart evidence of 'providence' language.

days.title: Comparing worldviews
days.work: Build a two-column comparison of the two texts' views of nature and community; vocabulary: build 10 cards from roots in the readings.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Timed paragraph: how does each text explain hardship? Cite two quotations each; quiz on Puritan terms.

weeks.assessment: Timed comparative paragraph scored on evidence and summary; vocabulary quiz.

objectives: Analyze figurative language and tone in Bradstreet and Edwards
materials: Bradstreet, 'To My Dear and Loving Husband', 'Upon the Burning of Our House'
Edwards, 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'

days.title: Bradstreet
days.work: Read two Bradstreet poems aloud; annotate the extended metaphors and identify the conflict between earthly and heavenly love.

days.title: Edwards' sermon
days.work: Read the first half of 'Sinners'; highlight imagery of spiders, fire, and flood and label each as an appeal.

days.title: Rhetorical appeals
days.work: Finish 'Sinners'; complete a SOAPSTone chart and explain why fear was an effective strategy for his audience.

days.title: Grammar: sentence variety
days.work: Analyze Edwards' long periodic sentences; rewrite three of your own sentences as periodic and cumulative sentences.

days.title: Seminar & check
days.work: Hold a recorded 15-minute discussion with a parent on 'Is fear a legitimate persuasive tool?'; submit a SOAPSTone analysis.

weeks.assessment: SOAPSTone chart and discussion rubric (evidence, building on ideas).

objectives: Analyze characterization and conflict in drama
materials: short video/article on the Red Scare

days.title: Context
days.work: Read a short article on the Salem trials of 1692 and one on the 1950s House Un-American Activities Committee; list parallels.

days.title: Act I
days.work: Read Act I aloud, taking several roles; track each character's motives (Abigail, Parris, Putnam, Proctor) in a chart.

days.title: Act I analysis
days.work: Write a paragraph on how Miller's stage directions shape Proctor before he speaks.

days.title: Act II
days.work: Read Act II; identify three moments of dramatic irony and explain the poppet's role in the plot.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz on Acts I–II and a one-paragraph prediction defended with evidence.

weeks.topic: The Crucible, Acts III–IV and literary argument

days.title: Act III
days.work: Read the courtroom act; trace how logic breaks down and cite the line where Hale turns.

days.title: Act IV
days.work: Read Act IV; discuss why Proctor refuses to sign and what 'my name' means; draft a thesis on integrity.

days.title: Two interpretations
days.work: Watch the courtroom scene from the 1996 film and compare to the script; note choices about Abigail's power.

days.title: Essay drafting
days.work: Write a 700-word literary argument: Is John Proctor a tragic hero? Include a counterclaim; edit for subject-verb agreement.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Revise essay with a checklist and take the Unit 1 test (passages from Edwards and Miller).

weeks.assessment: Literary argument essay (rubric) and Unit 1 test.

materials: Franklin, Autobiography excerpt (thirteen virtues) and Poor Richard's aphorisms (Gutenberg)

days.title: Autobiography
days.work: Read Franklin's 'project of arriving at moral perfection'; list his 13 virtues and mark his tone toward himself.

days.title: Aphorisms
days.work: Read 20 Poor Richard sayings; rewrite five in modern English and explain the reasoning each assumes.

days.title: Satire
days.work: Read 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America'; identify verbal irony and its target.

days.title: Expository writing
days.work: Track one personal virtue for three days Franklin-style and draft a 400-word reflective explanation.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Short-answer quiz on Enlightenment ideas and irony; submit the virtue reflection.

objectives: Analyze rhetorical structure of founding documents
Evaluate reasoning in seminal U.S. texts
materials: Paine, The Crisis No. 1 and Common Sense excerpt
Patrick Henry, Speech to the Virginia Convention

days.title: Common Sense & The Crisis
days.work: Read excerpts and label appeals and parallel structure; note how Paine addresses a mass audience.

days.title: Henry's speech
days.work: Read and deliver the final paragraph aloud; chart rhetorical questions, allusions, and their effect.

days.title: Declaration structure
days.work: Outline the Declaration as a syllogism (major premise, minor premise/grievances, conclusion).

days.title: Evaluating reasoning
days.work: Write a paragraph evaluating the strongest and weakest grievance as evidence; note who is excluded from 'all men'.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Compare two openings (Paine vs. Jefferson) in a timed 30-minute rhetorical paragraph.

weeks.topic: Rhetorical analysis essay: voices excluded and included
objectives: Write a full rhetorical analysis essay
Analyze Wheatley and Adams as counter-voices
materials: Phillis Wheatley, 'On Being Brought from Africa to America' and letter to Samson Occom

days.title: Wheatley
days.work: Read Wheatley's poem and Occom letter; analyze how she uses her audience's own beliefs to argue for freedom.

days.title: Abigail Adams
days.work: Read 'Remember the Ladies'; identify tone shifts and the argument beneath the playful diction.

days.title: Essay plan
days.work: Choose one founding-era text and outline a rhetorical analysis essay (situation, choices, effect).

days.title: Draft & edit
days.work: Write a 750-word rhetorical analysis; punctuation focus: semicolons and colons with quoted evidence.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Revise and submit essay; Unit 2 test on rhetorical terms and an unseen passage (Washington's Farewell Address excerpt).

weeks.assessment: Rhetorical analysis essay and Unit 2 test.

objectives: Identify characteristics of Romanticism and Gothic fiction
materials: Poe, 'The Fall of the House of Usher', 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

days.title: Romantic traits
days.work: Take notes on Romantic traits; read 'The Devil and Tom Walker' and mark satire of greed.

days.title: Poe's narrator
days.work: Read 'The Tell-Tale Heart'; annotate evidence the narrator is unreliable and chart sentence length vs. tension.

days.title: House of Usher
days.work: Read 'The Fall of the House of Usher'; trace setting as a symbol of Roderick's mind.

days.title: Structure
days.work: Write an analytical paragraph on how Poe's choice of ending structure produces 'unity of effect'.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on Romantic/Gothic conventions; one-paragraph comparison of Irving's and Poe's narrators.

objectives: Determine central ideas of Transcendentalist essays
materials: Thoreau, Walden ('Where I Lived...') and 'Civil Disobedience'

days.title: Emerson
days.work: Read excerpts of 'Self-Reliance'; select five aphorisms and explain each in plain language.

days.title: Nature
days.work: Read the 'transparent eyeball' passage from 'Nature'; take a 20-minute solo nature walk and write a journal entry in imitation.

days.title: Walden
days.work: Read 'Where I Lived, and What I Lived For'; list Thoreau's arguments for simplicity and test one against your own daily schedule.

days.title: Civil Disobedience
days.work: Read excerpts; trace how Thoreau refines the term 'government' and connect to later activists.

days.title: Seminar & check
days.work: Socratic seminar: 'Would Thoreau approve of smartphones?'; write a 300-word argument response.

weeks.assessment: Seminar participation rubric and short argument.

objectives: Compare Romantic and Dark Romantic views of human nature
materials: Hawthorne, 'Young Goodman Brown' and 'The Minister's Black Veil'

days.title: Young Goodman Brown
days.work: Read and annotate symbols (Faith's ribbons, staff, forest); decide whether the journey was a dream.

days.title: Black Veil
days.work: Read 'The Minister's Black Veil'; chart the community's reactions and explain the veil's meaning in a paragraph.

days.title: Bartleby I
days.work: Read the first half of 'Bartleby'; analyze the narrator's attitude and the phrase 'I would prefer not to'.

days.title: Bartleby II
days.work: Finish the story; compare Bartleby's refusal to Thoreau's civil disobedience in a T-chart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Timed essay (40 min): How do two Dark Romantic texts challenge Emerson's optimism?

weeks.topic: Poetry of a new nation: Whitman and Dickinson
objectives: Analyze form and style in poetry
materials: Whitman, 'Song of Myself' sections 1, 6, 52 and 'I Hear America Singing'
Dickinson, 'Because I could not stop for Death', 'Hope is the thing with feathers', 'Tell all the truth but tell it slant'

days.title: Whitman
days.work: Read 'Song of Myself' sections aloud; identify catalogs and anaphora and their effect.

days.title: Dickinson
days.work: Read four Dickinson poems; scan meter, mark dashes and slant rhymes, and paraphrase each.

days.title: Comparison
days.work: Plan a comparison of how Whitman and Dickinson treat death or the self; collect six quotations.

days.title: Write
days.work: Draft a 600-word poetry comparison essay, then memorize and recite one poem (12+ lines).

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Submit revised essay and take the Unit 3 test on Romantic and Transcendentalist texts.

weeks.assessment: Poetry comparison essay, recitation, Unit 3 test.

weeks.topic: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Ch. 1–6
objectives: Analyze how Douglass develops central ideas
Evaluate rhetorical purpose of a slave narrative

days.title: Context & preface
days.work: Read Garrison's preface and Douglass' Ch. 1; note how prefaces were used to authenticate narratives.

days.title: Ch. 2–4
days.work: Read and record examples of slavery's effect on enslavers as well as the enslaved.

days.title: Ch. 5–6
days.work: Read about Baltimore and learning letters; explain why Douglass calls literacy 'the pathway from slavery to freedom'.

days.title: Close reading
days.work: Analyze one paragraph's diction and syntax (balanced sentences, antithesis) in a 300-word response.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz Ch. 1–6 and central-idea tracker check.

objectives: Compare male and female slave narratives
materials: Harriet Jacobs, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl excerpts (Gutenberg)

days.title: Ch. 7–9
days.work: Read; identify how learning to read changes Douglass' self-understanding.

days.title: Ch. 10
days.work: Read the Covey chapter; analyze the chiasmus 'You have seen how a man was made a slave...' and its placement.

days.title: Ch. 11 & Appendix
days.work: Finish the Narrative; explain why Douglass withholds escape details and how the appendix addresses religion.

days.title: Harriet Jacobs
days.work: Read the 'loophole of retreat' excerpt; compare Jacobs' appeals to women readers with Douglass' appeals.

days.title: Discussion & check
days.work: Recorded discussion comparing the two narratives; written exit response on structure.

weeks.assessment: Discussion rubric and comparative exit response.

weeks.topic: Oratory of the Civil War era
objectives: Analyze structure and rhetoric of speeches
materials: Douglass, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'
Sojourner Truth, 'Ain't I a Woman?' (both versions)
Lincoln, Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural

days.title: Fourth of July speech
days.work: Read the central section; chart how Douglass turns the audience's celebration into an indictment.

days.title: Sojourner Truth
days.work: Compare the 1851 Robinson transcription with the 1863 Gage version; discuss how editing changed her voice.

days.title: Lincoln
days.work: Read the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural; mark antithesis and biblical allusion and explain the shift in purpose.

days.title: Deliver a speech
days.work: Memorize and deliver the Gettysburg Address or a 2-minute excerpt with deliberate pauses; self-evaluate from video.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Timed rhetorical analysis (40 min) of the Second Inaugural.

weeks.assessment: Speech delivery rubric and timed rhetorical analysis.

objectives: Write an evidence-based argument synthesizing multiple texts

days.title: Prompt & claim
days.work: Respond to 'Did the founding documents contain the seeds of abolition?' Draft a claim and gather evidence from three Unit 4 texts.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Build an outline with claim, reasons, evidence, warrants, and a counterclaim with rebuttal.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Write a 900-word argument essay; grammar focus: parallel structure in thesis and topic sentences.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Peer/parent review with a rubric; revise for warrants and transitions; edit for comma splices.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Submit the final essay and take the Unit 4 test (unseen passage from Lincoln-Douglas debates).

materials: Twain, 'The Notorious Jumping Frog of Calaveras County'
Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn Ch. 1, 16, 31 (Gutenberg)

days.title: Realism intro
days.work: Notes on Realism vs. Romanticism; read 'The Jumping Frog' (a California story) and identify the frame narrative.

days.title: Huck Finn Ch. 1 & 16
days.work: Read; analyze how Huck's vernacular voice creates humor and irony.

days.title: Ch. 31 'All right, then, I'll go to hell'
days.work: Read the climax of Huck's conscience; explain the irony of his decision.

days.title: Debating Huck Finn
days.work: Read two short critical views on teaching the novel; write a 300-word position response.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on Realism terms and satire; paragraph on the irony in Ch. 31.

objectives: Analyze how authors develop and relate story elements
Analyze irony and point of view
materials: Kate Chopin, 'The Story of an Hour'
Ambrose Bierce, 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge'

days.title: Chopin
days.work: Read 'The Story of an Hour'; annotate the open window imagery and explain the final irony.

days.title: Bierce
days.work: Read 'Owl Creek Bridge'; diagram the three-part structure and analyze the manipulation of time.

days.title: Gilman
days.work: Read 'The Yellow Wallpaper'; track the narrator's changing descriptions of the wallpaper.

days.title: London
days.work: Read 'To Build a Fire'; identify Naturalist ideas about nature and fate; compare to Emerson's 'Nature'.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 600-word explanatory essay on how two of these authors use structure to create a surprise ending.

days.title: Timeline review
days.work: Build a literary-period timeline (Puritan to Realism) with two texts, traits, and a key quotation per period.

days.title: Practice passages
days.work: Complete a practice set of unseen prose and poetry passages with multiple choice and short response.

days.title: Writing review
days.work: Revise the weakest essay of the semester using teacher comments; write a reflection on growth.

days.title: Semester exam I
days.work: Reading section: three unseen passages with multiple-choice and short constructed responses.

days.title: Semester exam II
days.work: Timed 50-minute synthesis essay: how American writers defined freedom from Bradford to Chopin.

weeks.assessment: Two-part semester exam and revised essay portfolio.

weeks.topic: Modernism and the poetry of disillusionment
materials: T.S. Eliot, 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'
Ezra Pound, 'In a Station of the Metro'
Robert Frost, 'Mending Wall' and 'The Road Not Taken'

days.title: Modernism intro
days.work: Notes on WWI, urbanization, and Modernism; read Imagist poems by Pound and Williams and write two Imagist poems of your own.

days.title: Prufrock I
days.work: Read 'Prufrock' aloud; annotate the fog/cat image and the refrain about Michelangelo.

days.title: Prufrock II
days.work: Analyze fragmentation and allusion; write a paragraph on Prufrock's paralysis.

days.title: Frost
days.work: Read 'Mending Wall' and 'The Road Not Taken'; argue about the commonly misread meaning of the 'road' poem.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on Modernist traits and a short poetry explication of an unseen Frost poem.

objectives: Trace symbols of the American Dream
materials: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (Gutenberg/public domain)

days.title: Context
days.work: Read a short Jazz Age/Prohibition overview; read Ch. 1 and analyze Nick's claim that he is 'inclined to reserve all judgments'.

days.title: Ch. 1 symbols
days.work: Analyze the green light and East/West Egg geography; start a symbol tracker.

days.title: Ch. 2
days.work: Read the Valley of Ashes chapter; explain the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg.

days.title: Ch. 3
days.work: Read Gatsby's party; collect rumors about Gatsby and evaluate Nick's reliability.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz Ch. 1–3 and a paragraph on setting as social commentary.

days.title: Ch. 4–5
days.work: Read; analyze Gatsby's invented biography and the reunion scene's use of weather.

days.title: Ch. 6–7
days.work: Read; trace the confrontation at the Plaza and how money divides 'old' and 'new' wealth.

days.title: Ch. 8–9
days.work: Finish the novel; annotate the final page's 'boats against the current' passage.

days.title: Interpretations
days.work: Compare the 1974 and 2013 party or ending scenes; evaluate how each interprets Fitzgerald.

days.title: Essay & check
days.work: Write a 900-word literary argument: Is The Great Gatsby a critique or a celebration of the American Dream?

objectives: Analyze voice and form in Harlem Renaissance poetry and fiction
Connect art to the Great Migration
materials: Langston Hughes, 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'Harlem', 'I, Too'
Zora Neale Hurston, 'How It Feels to Be Colored Me'

days.title: Hughes
days.work: Read three Hughes poems; listen to a blues recording and identify blues structure in 'The Weary Blues'.

days.title: McKay & Cullen
days.work: Read 'If We Must Die' (sonnet) and 'Incident'; compare how traditional forms carry protest.

days.title: Hurston
days.work: Read 'How It Feels to Be Colored Me'; analyze tone and figurative language.

days.title: Presentation prep
days.work: Research one Harlem Renaissance artist (writer, musician, painter) and build a 5-slide presentation.

days.title: Present & check
days.work: Deliver a 5-minute multimedia presentation and answer questions; quiz on the poems.

weeks.topic: Hemingway, Faulkner, and the Modern short story
objectives: Analyze style (iceberg theory, stream of consciousness)

days.title: Hemingway
days.work: Read 'Hills Like White Elephants'; list what is never stated and infer the conflict from dialogue alone.

days.title: Faulkner
days.work: Read 'A Rose for Emily'; reconstruct the chronology on a timeline and explain the effect of the nonlinear order.

days.title: Narrator 'we'
days.work: Analyze the communal narrator in 'Emily' and how it builds suspense.

days.title: Style imitation
days.work: Write a 500-word scene in Hemingway's minimalist style using only dialogue and gesture.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Unit 6 test: unseen Modernist passage analysis plus terms.

materials: public library databases (e.g., JSTOR free articles, Gale via library card)

days.title: Choose a topic
days.work: Brainstorm topics linking an American author to historical context; narrow to an arguable research question.

days.title: Library databases
days.work: Use public library databases to locate at least six sources, including two scholarly articles.

days.title: Evaluate sources
days.work: Apply the CRAAP test to each source and discard weak ones.

days.title: Annotated bibliography
days.work: Write MLA 9 entries with 3-sentence annotations for five sources.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit research question, working thesis, and annotated bibliography for feedback.

days.title: Note-taking
days.work: Take notes using quotation, paraphrase, and summary, labeling each with source and page.

days.title: Paraphrase practice
days.work: Practice paraphrasing three tricky passages and compare with originals to avoid patchwriting.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Build a detailed outline with thesis, sub-claims, and assigned evidence.

days.title: Draft I
days.work: Draft introduction and first two body sections (about 1,000 words) with signal phrases and in-text citations.

days.title: Draft II & check
days.work: Draft remaining sections and conclusion; submit full rough draft (1,800–2,200 words).

days.title: Revision for argument
days.work: Reverse-outline the draft; revise so each paragraph advances the thesis.

days.title: Line editing
days.work: Edit for concision, active voice, and varied syntax; check hyphenation of compound modifiers.

days.title: Format
days.work: Format to MLA 9 with Works Cited; run a self-check for plagiarism and citation accuracy.

days.title: Presentation
days.work: Create a 6-minute presentation of findings with visuals and practice delivery.

days.title: Final & present
days.work: Submit final research paper and deliver the presentation with Q&A.

weeks.assessment: Final research paper and presentation rubrics.

weeks.topic: A Raisin in the Sun, Acts I–II
objectives: Analyze character and conflict in drama
Connect the play to housing discrimination history
materials: Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun (library)

days.title: Context
days.work: Reread 'Harlem'; read a short article on redlining and restrictive covenants in Chicago.

days.title: Act I
days.work: Read Act I; chart each Younger family member's dream and conflicts.

days.title: Act I analysis
days.work: Analyze Mama's plant as a symbol in a paragraph with two quotations.

days.title: Act II
days.work: Read Act II; analyze Karl Lindner's visit and his euphemistic language.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz and a character foil chart (Walter vs. Beneatha).

weeks.topic: A Raisin in the Sun, Act III and performance

days.title: Act III
days.work: Read Act III; trace Walter's transformation and what 'come into his manhood' means.

days.title: Compare productions
days.work: Watch the 1961 film's final scene and compare it to the script's stage directions.

days.title: Scene work
days.work: Rehearse and perform a 3-minute scene with family members, focusing on subtext.

days.title: Theme essay
days.work: Write a 600-word essay on how Hansberry answers Hughes' question 'What happens to a dream deferred?'

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit essay; short test on the play.

objectives: Analyze rhetoric and reasoning in seminal civil rights texts
materials: Martin Luther King Jr., 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'
Malcolm X, 'The Ballot or the Bullet' excerpt

days.title: Kennedy
days.work: Read/listen to the Inaugural Address; mark antimetabole and parallel structure.

days.title: Letter I
days.work: Read the first half of 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'; outline how King rebuts each criticism from the clergymen.

days.title: Letter II
days.work: Finish the Letter; analyze King's definition of just and unjust laws and his appeal to Founders.

days.title: Malcolm X
days.work: Read 'The Ballot or the Bullet' excerpt; compare purpose and audience with King.

days.title: Check
days.work: Timed rhetorical analysis essay (40 min) on an excerpt from the Letter.

weeks.topic: Personal narrative and the college essay

days.title: Models
days.work: Read two model personal essays (e.g., Amy Tan's 'Mother Tongue' as a model of voice); note structure and reflection.

days.title: Brainstorm
days.work: Read the UC Personal Insight Questions; brainstorm with a memory map and choose two prompts.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft a 350-word response focused on a single scene and what it reveals.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise for specificity and reflection; cut clichés; read aloud for voice.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit a polished personal insight essay and write a second draft for another prompt.

weeks.topic: War and memory: The Things They Carried
objectives: Analyze structure and truth in fiction
materials: Tim O'Brien, The Things They Carried (library) – title story, 'On the Rainy River', 'How to Tell a True War Story'

days.title: Title story
days.work: Read 'The Things They Carried'; chart tangible vs. intangible burdens.

days.title: Rainy River
days.work: Read 'On the Rainy River'; analyze the choice between courage and shame.

days.title: True war story
days.work: Read 'How to Tell a True War Story'; define story-truth vs. happening-truth.

days.title: Interviews
days.work: Watch a veteran interview from the Library of Congress Veterans History Project; compare oral history to fiction.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a 500-word response analyzing how O'Brien's structure blurs fact and fiction.

objectives: Analyze how authors use language to explore identity
materials: Sandra Cisneros, The House on Mango Street (selected vignettes)
Gloria Anzaldúa, 'How to Tame a Wild Tongue' excerpt

days.title: Tan
days.work: Read 'Mother Tongue'; list the 'Englishes' she describes and evaluate her argument about language and judgment.

days.title: Cisneros
days.work: Read six Mango Street vignettes; analyze how compressed form conveys identity.

days.title: Rodriguez & Anzaldúa
days.work: Read excerpts; compare positions on public and private language.

days.title: Write a vignette
days.work: Write two Cisneros-style vignettes about your own neighborhood or name.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write an 800-word analytical essay comparing two authors' views on language and identity.

weeks.topic: Contemporary poetry and Native American voices
materials: Joy Harjo, 'Remember' and 'Perhaps the World Ends Here'
Natalie Diaz, 'The Facts of Art' (Poetry Foundation)

days.title: Harjo
days.work: Read two Harjo poems; analyze repetition and the connection between land and identity.

days.title: Lee & Dove
days.work: Read 'Persimmons' and 'Testimonial'; trace imagery of fruit, memory, and language.

days.title: Diaz
days.work: Read 'The Facts of Art'; discuss how humor and history combine in the poem.

days.title: Performance prep
days.work: Choose a contemporary American poem and prepare an oral interpretation with a written introduction.

days.title: Check
days.work: Perform the poem (recorded) and submit a 300-word explication.

weeks.topic: Argument and media: the American Dream today
objectives: Synthesize multiple sources in different media
materials: Pew Research Center short reports on economic mobility
two op-eds on the American Dream
a TED talk or podcast segment

days.title: Sources
days.work: Read two op-eds and a data report on economic mobility; annotate claims and evidence quality.

days.title: Media
days.work: Watch or listen to a talk; evaluate the speaker's evidence and rhetoric with an SL.3 checklist.

days.title: Plan
days.work: Outline a synthesis argument using at least four sources, including one literary text from the year.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Write a 900-word synthesis essay: 'Is the American Dream still achievable?'

days.title: Check
days.work: Revise and submit; Unit 9 vocabulary and grammar test (usage, hyphenation, punctuation).

objectives: Curate and reflect on a writing portfolio

days.title: Thematic threads
days.work: Choose a theme (freedom, identity, the frontier, dissent) and map it across six texts from different periods.

days.title: Portfolio selection
days.work: Select four best pieces and revise one substantially.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Write a 600-word reflective letter on growth as reader and writer.

days.title: Publish
days.work: Build a digital portfolio site with pieces, reflection, and a reading list.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present portfolio and thematic map to family in a 10-minute talk.

objectives: Demonstrate year-long reading, writing, and language mastery

days.title: Review I
days.work: Review literary periods and key rhetorical terms with a self-made study guide and flashcards.

days.title: Review II
days.work: Practice an unseen poem and a nonfiction passage with timed responses.

days.title: Final exam I
days.work: Reading comprehension: unseen literary and informational passages with multiple-choice and short answers.

days.title: Final exam II
days.work: Timed 60-minute argument essay drawing on at least three texts from the year.

days.title: Wrap-up
days.work: Review exam results, set summer reading goals, and choose three books for senior year.
